questions.q: Ohm's law relates which three quantities?
If the voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled, what happens to the current through it?
A 6 Ω resistor carries a current of 2 A. What voltage is across it?
A resistor dissipates 20 W while carrying 5 A. What is its resistance?
"More resistance always means less current." Under what condition is this actually true?
options: Only when the voltage across that resistor is held constant

questions.q: KCL states that at any node, the sum of currents entering equals:
options: Zero always, regardless of currents leaving

questions.q: KVL (sum of voltages around a loop = 0) is a direct consequence of which conservation principle?
In a single loop, a 20 V source drives current through a 2 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in series. Find the loop current.
At a node, 5 A and 3 A flow in, and two currents I1 and I2 flow out with I1 = 6 A. What is I2?
Why can KCL never be 'violated' at an ideal node, even momentarily?
options: Because charge cannot accumulate at a point with zero capacitance
Because current always flows in one direction

questions.q: For two resistors in parallel, the equivalent resistance is:
Why do parallel resistors always share the same voltage?
options: Because they are connected between the same pair of nodes
Because they carry the same current
Because KVL forbids different voltages anywhere

questions.q: R1=4 Ω and R2=12 Ω are in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.
In a current divider with R1=2 Ω and R2=8 Ω fed by 10 A, which resistor carries the larger current, and why?
options: R1, because the current-divider share is weighted by the OTHER resistor
R2, because larger resistance always gets more current
R1, because it is closer to the source

questions.q: A student writes the current-divider formula for I(R2) as I×R2/(R1+R2), copying the voltage-divider pattern. What is wrong?
options: The numerator should be R1 (the other resistor), not R2
The formula needs voltage, not current, as I

questions.q: In node-voltage analysis, the first step is always to:
options: Convert all sources to Norton form

questions.q: Node-voltage analysis writes one equation per unknown node using which law?
A single node has a 6 A source injecting current and one 3 Ω resistor to ground. Find the node voltage.
In a 2-node circuit, node B's equation simplifies to V_B = V_A/4. If V_A is later found to be 16 V, what is V_B?
For a circuit with many parallel branches and current sources but few loops, which method is generally more efficient?
options: Neither — trial and error is required

questions.q: Mesh-current analysis assigns a circulating current to each:
A resistor shared between two meshes carries a current equal to:
options: The difference of the two mesh currents
The sum of the two mesh currents
The larger of the two mesh currents

questions.q: Two mesh equations are 6I1−2I2=16 and −2I1+8I2=2. Find I1.
Using the previous question's I1=3 A, and I2=1 A, what is the actual current through the shared resistor?
Mesh-current analysis is best suited to circuits that are:
options: Planar, with many series loops and voltage sources

questions.q: A voltage source Vs in series with R transforms into a current source of value:
options: Vs/R, in parallel with the same R

questions.q: Two sources are 'externally indistinguishable' if they produce the same:
A 12 V source in series with a 4 Ω resistor is transformed. What is the equivalent current source value?
After transforming a 20 V/5 Ω source to current form, what is the short-circuit current predicted by the ORIGINAL voltage-source form?
Source transformation is most useful for:
options: Simplifying a network before applying node or mesh analysis
Measuring actual internal source resistance physically
Eliminating the need for Kirchhoff's laws entirely

questions.q: R_th is found by:
options: Killing all independent sources and finding resistance at the terminals
Adding all resistances in the circuit
Dividing V_th by the load current

questions.q: V_th is defined as the:
options: Open-circuit voltage at the terminals of interest

questions.q: A network has a 24 V source in series with 6 Ω, feeding a 12 Ω resistor to the terminals (load removed). Find V_th.
For the same network, with the 24 V source shorted, R_th (6 Ω parallel 12 Ω) equals:
Norton's current I_N relates to Thevenin's V_th and R_th by:
Maximum power is transferred to a load R_L when:
At the maximum-power-transfer condition, what is the efficiency of power delivery to the load?
V_th = 16 V, R_th = 4 Ω. Find the maximum power deliverable to a matched load.
Differentiating P = V_th²R_L/(R_th+R_L)² with respect to R_L and setting it to zero yields the factor:
Why do power-grid engineers deliberately AVOID the maximum-power-transfer condition (R_L=R_th)?
options: Because it wastes half the power in the source resistance, hurting efficiency
Because it makes the load explode
Because R_th is always unknown in a grid

questions.q: When applying superposition, an unused voltage source is replaced by:
options: A resistor equal to its internal resistance
Nothing — it is removed from the diagram entirely

questions.q: Superposition works only for circuits that are:
A node's voltage from a 24 V source alone is 16 V, and from a 2 A source alone is 8 V. What is the total node voltage with both active?
Why can't superposition be used directly to find POWER dissipated by an element in a multi-source circuit?
options: Power is proportional to current or voltage squared, which is not a linear operation
Power is always zero in linear circuits
Power doesn't depend on current or voltage

questions.q: Superposition is most valuable when you specifically need:
options: The individual contribution of each independent source to a given response
A faster way to compute total resistance
To eliminate all sources from the circuit

questions.q: A coil rotating at constant angular speed ω in a uniform magnetic field produces an EMF of the form:
One full mechanical rotation (360°) of the coil corresponds to:
options: One full cycle of the sine wave

questions.q: A coil produces a peak EMF at a shaft angle of 90°. At what angle does it next reach zero?
If the frequency f of rotation doubles, what happens to ω = 2πf?
The DC generator's commutator relates to this rotating-coil picture by:
options: Mechanically rectifying the AC waveform into a one-directional output
Removing the need for a magnetic field

b2.label: RMS, Average, Form Factor & Peak Factor

questions.q: The RMS value of a sinusoid with peak V_m is:
Why is the true average of a sine wave over a FULL cycle equal to zero?
options: Equal positive and negative areas cancel exactly
Because sine waves have no peak

questions.q: A sinusoidal voltage has V_m = 100 V. What is its RMS value?
Given V_rms=70.7 V and V_avg=63.7 V for the same waveform, what is the form factor (to 2 d.p.)?
A 230 V AC mains rating refers to which value of the waveform?
Impedance Z is defined as:
options: V/I in the phasor domain, Z=R+jX

questions.q: For a pure inductor, voltage and current are related by a phase difference of:
A pure capacitor has reactance X_C at 50 Hz. If the frequency doubles, X_C = 1/(ωC) will:
Why does differentiation become multiplication by jω in the phasor domain?
options: Because the derivative of a sinusoid is another sinusoid of the same frequency, scaled and phase-shifted by 90°
Because phasors are only valid for DC
Because Ohm's law does not apply to AC

questions.q: The main benefit of representing AC quantities as phasors is:
options: It turns differential equations into ordinary complex-number algebra
It removes the need for KVL and KCL
It only works for resistive circuits
It eliminates the concept of frequency

questions.q: In a series RL circuit, the current:
options: Is exactly in phase with voltage

questions.q: A series RLC circuit is at resonance (in phase, φ=0) exactly when:
A series RL circuit has R=3 Ω and X_L=4 Ω. Find the impedance magnitude |Z|.
For the same circuit (R=3 Ω, X_L=4 Ω) supplied at 50 V rms, find the current.
Why is the impedance triangle (R, X, Z) essentially the same picture as the phasor diagram of B3?
options: Because dividing the voltage phasor triangle by the common current gives exactly R, X and Z
Because impedance has no relationship to phasors
Because R and X are always numerically equal
Because it only applies to DC circuits

b5.label: Power & Power Factor in AC Circuits

questions.q: Real power in an AC circuit is given by:
Reactive power Q is best described as:
options: Power that oscillates between source and reactive elements without net dissipation
The same thing as apparent power
Power that only exists in DC circuits

questions.q: V=50 V, I=10 A, φ=53.13° (cosφ=0.6). Find the real power P.
For the same circuit, P=300 W and Q=400 VAR. Verify the apparent power S using S²=P²+Q².
A factory with a low power factor pays more even though reactive power isn't dissipated, because:
options: A lower cosφ demands a larger current for the same real power, requiring thicker cables and bigger transformers
Reactive power is billed at a higher rate by definition
Low power factor always damages equipment
It has no real financial effect

questions.q: Which DC motor part mechanically reverses current in the armature coils every half-turn?
The yoke of a DC motor serves which two purposes?
options: Supports the field poles and provides a path for magnetic flux
Generates back-EMF and cools the armature
Converts AC to DC and insulates the shaft
Produces torque directly and reduces friction

questions.q: Which component would you inspect first if a DC motor's armature current is not reaching the winding at all?
Why are armature and pole cores built from thin, insulated laminations rather than a solid block?
options: To increase electrical resistance of the core

questions.q: A pole shoe's curved surface primarily helps by:
options: Increasing cross-sectional area to reduce magnetic reluctance and supporting the field coil

c2.label: DC Motor: Working Principle & Back EMF

questions.q: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule finds the direction of:
options: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

questions.q: Why does a DC motor generate a back-EMF as soon as it starts turning?
options: The moving armature conductor is itself now cutting the field, exactly as in a generator
Back-EMF is externally applied by the supply
It only occurs at maximum speed
It occurs only in AC motors

questions.q: V=220 V, R_a=1 Ω, I_a=20 A. Find the back-EMF E_b.
For the same motor, find the mechanical power developed (E_b × I_a).
Why is it incorrect to call back-EMF 'wasted energy'?
options: Because E_b×I_a is exactly the mechanical power produced; only I_a²R_a is a true loss
Because it always equals the supply voltage
Because it only matters in transformers

questions.q: In a shunt DC motor, the field winding is connected:
options: Directly across a separate DC supply only
Not connected to the armature circuit at all

questions.q: Why must a series DC motor never be started with no mechanical load?
options: Very low flux at no load can let current and speed rise dangerously (runaway)
It will simply refuse to start
It converts to a generator instantly

questions.q: Which type of DC motor is most appropriate for cranes and traction applications needing high starting torque?
options: None of these types produce high starting torque

questions.q: A shunt motor maintains near-constant speed under varying load mainly because:
options: Its field flux is set by the fixed supply voltage, independent of load current
Its commutator spins at fixed speed regardless of torque

questions.q: A compound motor is best described as:
options: A deliberate blend of shunt and series characteristics, trading off their strengths
Identical in behaviour to a pure shunt motor
Identical in behaviour to a pure series motor
A motor with no field winding at all

questions.q: A transformer transfers energy between primary and secondary windings via:
options: A common magnetic flux, with no electrical connection between windings

questions.q: Why is the transformer core built of thin, insulated silicon-steel laminations?
options: To reduce eddy-current losses while silicon reduces hysteresis losses
To increase the core's electrical conductivity
To eliminate the need for windings
To increase the core's magnetic reluctance

questions.q: In core-type construction, where are the low-voltage and high-voltage windings typically placed relative to each other?
options: LV winding next to the core, HV winding over it, to reduce insulation requirements
HV winding always on a separate limb with no shared core
Both windings placed with no core between them
LV and HV windings are never on the same limb

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between core-type and shell-type transformer construction?
options: Shell-type surrounds the windings with a three-limb core; core-type has windings around two limbs of a rectangular core
Core-type has no magnetic core at all
There is no difference; the names are interchangeable

questions.q: Minimising the air-gap between core laminations is important because it:
options: Keeps the magnetising (excitation) current as low as possible
Has no effect on transformer performance
Converts the transformer into an inductor

questions.q: The transformer EMF equation is:
The constant 4.44 in the EMF equation arises from:
options: 2π/√2, converting angular frequency and peak flux into an RMS EMF
A rounding convention with no physical basis
The number of turns in a standard winding
The ratio of primary to secondary turns

questions.q: For the same transformer, E2=1110 V. Confirm the turns ratio N1/N2 matches E1/E2.
If N2 > N1 for a transformer, it is classified as:
options: Isolation only, neither step-up nor down

questions.q: The synchronous speed of a 3-phase induction motor is given by:
Why must the rotor of an induction motor always turn slightly SLOWER than the synchronous speed?
options: If it matched synchronous speed exactly, the field would stop cutting the rotor bars and no torque would be induced
The rotor is mechanically braked at all times
Synchronous speed is only a theoretical value, never achievable in any motor
The stator windings physically limit rotor speed

questions.q: A 4-pole motor is supplied at 50 Hz. Find its synchronous speed.
The same motor runs at 1440 rpm. Find the slip.
Compared to a wound (slip-ring) rotor, a squirrel-cage rotor is generally preferred when:
options: Low cost and low maintenance matter more than adjustable starting torque via external resistance
Very high starting torque with adjustable external resistance is required
Frequent speed control via rotor resistance is essential
The application demands brushes and slip rings
